title: Build a Computer Vision Workflow (Exercise)
text:
A pretrained model returns raw predictions — bounding boxes, class names, confidence scores. A real application usually needs more: filtering results, counting objects, drawing overlays, or triggering downstream actions.
A Workflow is Roboflow’s way of wiring those steps together visually. You connect blocks (model, filter, visualization, logic) into a pipeline, test it in a debugger, and deploy it through the Inference Server.

title: Roboflow Rapid (Exercise)
text:
Training a custom vision model usually means collecting data, labeling it, choosing hyperparameters, and waiting for training to finish. Roboflow Rapid compresses that loop into minutes: you upload images, annotate what you want the model to find, and Rapid trains a detector for you.
Rapid is the fastest way to answer a practical question: “Can a model learn to recognize my objects?” The result is a model you can test in the browser and deploy as an API — no local GPU required.

title: Interactive Neural Networks Playground (Exercise)
section: Activity 1: Discover Why We Need Non-Linearity
text:
Activity 1: Discover Why We Need Non-Linearity
Goal: Understand the limitations of simple linear models and why neural networks need activation functions.

Select the Dataset: Choose Gaussian (top right under Data).
Set Up the Network:


Features: Keep only \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) selected.
Hidden Layers: Set to 0 (no hidden layers).
Activation: Set to Linear.


Run: Click the Play button at the top left.


Result: The network easily draws a straight line separating the orange and blue dots.


Switch Dataset: Now select the Circle dataset. Hit Play again.


Observation: The straight line moves around, but it cannot separate the inner blue dots from the outer orange ring.


Fix it with Activation:


Add 1 Hidden Layer with 3 neurons.
Change Activation from Linear to ReLU or Tanh.
Hit Play.


Key Takeaway: Real-world data is rarely linearly separable. Adding hidden layers combined with non-linear activation functions (like ReLU or Tanh) allows the network to bend and curve its decision boundaries.

title: Interactive Neural Networks Playground (Exercise)
section: Activity 2: Feature Engineering vs. Deep Networks
text:
Activity 2: Feature Engineering vs. Deep Networks
Goal: Learn how giving a model better input features can simplify the network architecture.

Select the Dataset: Choose Circle.
Set Hidden Layers to 1.
Deselect \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) as features.
Select \(X_1^2\) and \(X_2^2\) instead.
Run: Click Play.


Key Takeaway: With the right features (\(X_1^2\) and \(X_2^2\) describe a circle mathematically: \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\)), a simple model without any hidden layers can solve a non-linear problem instantly. Deep learning reduces the need for manual feature engineering, but good features still make learning much easier.

title: Interactive Neural Networks Playground (Exercise)
text:
Activity 3: The “XOR” Problem (Combining Features)
Goal: Understand how hidden neurons combine simpler lines into complex geometric shapes.

Select the Dataset: Choose Exclusive OR (XOR) (four alternating quadrants).
Set Features: Select only \(X_1\) and \(X_2\).
Build the Network:


Add 1 Hidden Layer with 4 Neurons.
Set Activation to Tanh or ReLU.


Run and Pause: Hit Play, and as it converges, hover your mouse over each individual neuron in the hidden layer.


Key Takeaway: Each neuron in the hidden layer learns a distinct straight decision boundary. The final output layer combines these individual boundaries into a box/cross shape that solves the XOR problem.

title: Interactive Neural Networks Playground (Exercise)
text:
Activity 4: Conquer the “Spiral” (Handling Complex Data)
Goal: Experience how network depth and width impact learning capacity on hard problems.

Select the Dataset: Choose Spiral (bottom right dataset—the hardest one).
First Attempt (Underfitting): Try running it with 1 hidden layer and 2 neurons.


Observation: The network fails to learn the interweaving spirals.


Scale Up:


Add 3 to 4 Hidden Layers.
Put 6 to 8 Neurons in the first few layers.
Set Activation to ReLU or Tanh.
Set Learning Rate to 0.03.


Run: Watch the Test Loss and Training Loss numbers in the top-right graph.


Key Takeaway: Highly intricate patterns require greater network “capacity” (more layers and neurons) to learn the fine-grained curves of the data distribution.

title: Application of Clustering in Geospatial Analytics
text:
Geographic Names Data
Let’s explore clustering using geographic names data.
Create a table to hold the data. Note that the table is generating the points automatically from the longitude/latitude (EPSG:4326) and transforming into a planar projection for the USA (EPSG:5070).
CREATE TABLE geonames (
  geonameid integer,
  name text,
  asciiname text,
  alternatenames text,
  latitude float8,
  longitude float8,
  fclass char,
  fcode text,
  country text,
  cc2 text,
  admin1 text,
  admin2 text,
  admin3 text,
  admin4 text,
  population bigint,
  elevation integer,
  dem text,
  timezone text,
  modification date,
  geom geometry(point, 5070)
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS
      (ST_Transform(ST_Point(longitude, latitude, 4326),5070)) STORED
);
Now load the table. Note the super fun use of PROGRAM to pull data directly from the web and feed a COPY.
COPY geonames
  FROM PROGRAM '(curl http://download.geonames.org/export/dump/US.zip > /tmp/US.zip) && unzip -p /tmp/US.zip US.txt'
  WITH (FORMAT CSV, DELIMITER E'\t', HEADER false);
(This trick only works using the postgres superuser, since it involves calling a program and writing to system disk. If you do not have superuser access, download and unzip the US.TXT file by hand and load it using COPY from the file.)



USA schools


Finally, add a spatial index to the geom column.
CREATE INDEX geonames_geom_x
  ON geonames
  USING GIST (geom);

title: Application of Clustering in Geospatial Analytics
text:
Schools
There are 434 distinct feature codes in the geonames table. We will restrict our analysis to just the 205,848 schools, with an fcode of SCH.
SELECT Count(DISTINCT fcode) FROM geonames;
SELECT Count(fcode) FROM geonames WHERE fcode = 'SCH';
Schools are an interesting feature to analyze because there’s a nice strong correlation between the number of schools and the population. There’s a lot of schools! But they are not uniformly distributed.



Midwest schools


If we zoom into the midwest, the concentration of schools in populated places pops out. We can use PostGIS to turn this distribution difference into a data set of populated places!

title: Application of Clustering in Geospatial Analytics
text:
Clustering on Schools
The DBSCAN clustering algorithm is a “density based spatial clustering of applications with noise”. The PostGIS ST_ClusterDBSCAN implementation is a window function that takes three parameters:

The geometries to be analyzed for clusters.
A ‘eps’ distance tolerance. Geometries must be within this distance to be added to a cluster.
A ‘minpoints’ count. If a point is within the ‘eps’ distance of ‘minpoints’ cluster members, it is a “core member” of the cluster.

An input geometry is added to a cluster if it is either:

A “core” geometry, that is within eps distance of at least minpoints input geometries (including itself); or
A “border” geometry, that is within eps distance of a core geometry.

How does this play out in practice?
If we zoom further into Chicago, around the suburban/exurban transition, the schools are about 1000 meters apart, sometimes more sometimes less, transitioning out to 2000 meters and more in the exurbs.



exurban school map


For our clusters, we will use:

A eps distance of 2000m
A minpoints of 5
A partition on the state code (admin1) to cut down on the number of cluster numbers.

CREATE TABLE geonames_sch AS
  SELECT ST_ClusterDBScan(geom, 2000, 5)
           OVER (PARTITION BY admin1) AS cluster, *
  FROM geonames
  WHERE fcode = 'SCH';
The result looks like this, with each cluster given a distinct color, and un-clustered schools rendered transparent.



Midwest schools


The smaller clusters look a little arbitrary, but if we zoom in, we can see that even small population centers have been surfaced with this analytical technique.
Here is Kanakee, Illinois, neatly identified as a populated place by its cluster of schools.



Kanakee

title: Application of Clustering in Geospatial Analytics
text:
Clusters to Points
Now that we have clusters, getting a populated place point is as simple as using the ST_Centroid function.
CREATE TABLE geonames_popplaces AS
  SELECT ST_Centroid(ST_Collect(geom))::geometry(Point, 5070) AS geom,
         Count(*) AS school_count,
         cluster, admin1
  FROM geonames_sch
  GROUP BY cluster, admin1
We have completed the analysis, converting the density difference in school locations into a set of derived populated place points.



Kanakee


Now for the whole population cluster map!



US Pop map

title: Application of Clustering in Geospatial Analytics
text:
Quick recap

Create a table ST_ClusterDBScan

Set an eps for distance tolerance
Set a minpoints to reduce density
Partition on a different field to cut down on the number of cluster numbers.

Create a final table using the ST_Centroid

title: Coding Agent Exercise
text:
Ensure you have a new project repo open with a Coding Agent.
Here is the requirements for the Recipe Manager project:
# Recipe Manager

## Problem Statement

Create a digital recipe book that allows users to store, retrieve, and manage your favorite recipes through a Python application that stores data in a .csv file.

## User Stories

1. When I start up the application, I am given the following options:
1. Add a new recipe to the collection
2. Search for recipes by ingredient
3. View all recipes
4. View a random recipe suggestion
2. If I choose to add a new recipe, I am asked to provide:
1. The recipe name
2. A list of ingredients separated by commas
3. Preparation time in minutes
4. Cooking instructions
5. Difficulty level (Easy, Medium, Hard)
3. If I choose to search by ingredient:
1. The program asks for an ingredient to search for
2. The program displays all recipes that contain that ingredient
4. If I choose to view all recipes:
1. The program displays a list of all recipe names with their preparation times
5. If I choose to get a random recipe suggestion:
1. The program randomly selects and displays a complete recipe from the collection

## Technical Requirements

- Stores all recipes in a .csv file
- Loads previously created recipes when the user initializes the application

## Stretch Goals - Mandatory

1. The program allows you to categorize recipes (Breakfast, Lunch, Dinner, Dessert)
2. The program can scale ingredient quantities based on desired number of servings
3. The program allows users to rate recipes and sort by rating
4. The program can generate a shopping list based on selected recipes
5. The program can track cooking history and suggest recipes you haven't made recently
To effectively construct big projects like this, you want to write prompts like this:

Prompt 1


Plan

Let's plan the project with the following requirements:

{INSERT PROJECT REQUIREMENTS HERE}



Prompt 2


Plan

Let's break down the plan into phases.
Within each phase let's make sure the tasks are independent such that multiple agents can execute them in parallel.



Prompt 3
You may decide to change the stack or theme or something


Plan

Backend: Flask and sqlite3 for the database
Frontend: Tailwind css

title: Run a YOLO Model (Exercise)
text:
YOLO (You Only Look Once) is a family of real-time computer vision models. Instead of scanning an image in multiple passes, YOLO processes the whole image at once and returns predictions in a single forward pass — which is why it is fast enough for live video.
Ultralytics YOLO26 is the latest generation in this family. One pretrained checkpoint can be swapped to different task heads — detection, classification, segmentation, pose estimation, and more — without changing the overall workflow.
If you attended the lecture, revisit Introduction to Computer Vision Tasks for the full task list and examples.

title: Supervision (Exercise)
text: Supervision is the library used for post-processing, which is done in the on_prediction(...) function.

title: Supervision (Exercise)
text:
Your Task
Goal: Use Supervision to turn raw model predictions into something useful — annotations, tracks, or counts — by running one of the tutorials below in your own code.
Pick one of the tutorials below and run it in your code:

detect and annotate objects on images,
track objects across video,
count objects in zones,
count line crossings,
build task-specific analytics such as parking occupancy.
